new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word; secondary stress on the third, fifth.. syllables counting from the left, but never on a final syllable (so 3-syllable words have a single stress). Quantity-insensitive; the language has no monosyllabic words (Hayes p.48; StressTyp2 'no monosyllables').
new_statements.secondary_stress: On odd-numbered non-final syllables from the left (10200, 102020); no final stress (Hayes 1995:199; Kager 1995 (6a): 'no sub-minimal words, no final stresses'; StressTyp2: i2@1L, no 1R).
new_statements.exceptions: None reported in the second-hand sources. Note that Holmer 1983 (Bidjara sketch, p.205; Part I p.6), an independent but impressionistic survey of the sister dialect Bidjara, says stress is 'not significant' and that longer words tend to accent the second syllable with alternating secondaries — a contradiction of the Breen/Hayes pattern, but about Bidjara and not Gungabula.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level description in Hayes' typological summary of Breen 1973; Breen's grammar treats Bidyara and Gungabula as one language with two dialects, so the statement is for the Bidyara/Gungabula complex, not Gungabula specifically. Second-hand: the Google Books snippet is what is held by the project; Breen's own wording and page are unknown.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog splits Gungabula (gung1248, AIATSIS E35) from Bidyara/Bidjara (bidy1243, E37), but the sole primary description, Breen 1973, treats them as two dialects of one language ('Bidyara and Gungabula'), and every second-hand stress statement (Hayes 1995:199, StressTyp2 lect 'Bidyara/Gungabula', Kager 1995, Gordon 2002) is for the joint Bidyara/Gungabula complex, not for Gungabula alone. Breen's Gungabula data came from a few speakers recorded c.1967-72 at Augathella/Clermont (AIAS tape listings name Jimmy Lawton, Kruger Fraser, Mick Tatton). Holmer 1983's Bidjara sketch (pp. 202-218; stress remark p.205) is a separate, impressionistic description of Bidjara (bidy1243) with no Gungabula informant and gives a conflicting picture (stress 'not significant', tendency to second-syllable accent). Stress data for the sister languages Margany/Gunya (Breen 1981:295-296) are already held under guny1241.
